procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated August 9, 1967, of the Patna High Court in Criminal Writ Jurisdiction Case No. 31 of 1967, dismissing the appellant's application for a writ of habeas corpus.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The appellant (Rameshwar Lal Patwari) applied to the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution and Section 491 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for a writ of habeas corpus, seeking release from detention. He challenged the grounds of detention, arguing they were either non-existent, vague, or irrelevant. The High Court scrutinized the grounds and dismissed his petition.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellant appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave, challenging the High Court's conclusion. He urged the same contentions as he did in the High Court.

issue.issue_text: Whether the court can scrutinize the material on which the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is based, even if it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds.

facts: The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on grounds including alleged black-marketing.
The grounds supplied to the appellant were challenged as being vague, non-existent, or false.
Specifically, one ground referred to a pending case against the appellant, when in fact he had been tried and acquitted months earlier.
Other grounds were found to be vague or based on flimsy excuses.
law: The formation of the opinion for detention rests on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, and courts are not an appellate authority to judge the sufficiency of the grounds.
However, detention without trial is a serious matter that requires the "closest scrutiny of the material on which the decision is formed."
The grounds for detention must not be vague or indefinite, as this would deny the detenu a real opportunity to make a representation.
If a vital ground is shown to be non-existent, false, or irrelevant, it vitiates the entire detention order.
The court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the authority by holding that the remaining valid grounds are sufficient to sustain the detention.
application: The Court acknowledged its limited role, stating it could not decide if the grounds were "good or bad" or assess their impact on the detaining authority's mind.
Despite this, it asserted its duty to scrutinize the material. It found that the detaining authority had acted with a "disregard for truth and accuracy."
The Court identified that referring to an acquitted case as a pending one was a serious error, demonstrating that due care and attention had not been paid.
It concluded that since some grounds were non-existent (the false claim of a pending case) and others were vague, the entire detention order was flawed.

The Court reasoned that if one of several grounds is found to be illusory or non-existent, the entire order is vitiated because it is impossible for the court to know to what extent that faulty ground influenced the authority's subjective satisfaction.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that while it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds for detention, it must closely scrutinize the material on which the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction is based. If any of the grounds are found to be vague, non-existent, or false, the entire detention order is vitiated, as the court cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the executive authority.

issue.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be sustained if one of the grounds supplied is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant.

facts: The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on several grounds, including alleged black-marketing.
Upon review, the Court found that some of the grounds provided were defective.
Specifically, at least two grounds were found to be vague, and one was false.
The false ground referred to a pending case against the appellant, when in fact he had been tried and acquitted months earlier.
law: The decision to detain a person is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority, and courts cannot act as an appellate authority to judge the sufficiency of the grounds.
However, because detention without trial is a serious matter, the material used to form this satisfaction must be scrutinized closely.
If one of several grounds for detention is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant, the entire detention order is vitiated (invalidated).
Grounds for detention must not be vague or indefinite, as this would deny the detenu a real opportunity to make an effective representation against the detention.
application: The Court reasoned that it is impossible to assess how much each individual ground contributed to the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction.
If one ground is invalid, the Court cannot simply assume the authority would have been satisfied based on the remaining grounds.
To do so would be to substitute the court's own objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive authority, which is contrary to the law.
In this case, the presence of vague and false grounds (like the acquitted case being cited as pending) demonstrated a lack of care and attention by the detaining authority.
Because some of the grounds were non-existent and others were too vague for the appellant to make an effective representation, the entire basis for the detention was compromised.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that a detention order cannot be sustained if one of the grounds supplied is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant. The entire order is vitiated because it is impossible to determine whether the detaining authority would have made the same decision without the invalid ground, and upholding it would substitute the court's judgment for the authority's subjective satisfaction.

issue.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention supplied to the appellant were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, or based on carelessness.

facts: The appellant was detained under the Preventive Detention Act, 1950, on the grounds that he was engaged in the black-marketing of food grains.
The grounds of detention supplied to the appellant contained several defects.

One ground stated that a case was pending against the appellant, but he had actually been tried and acquitted in that case months earlier. The court noted this showed a 'disregard for truth and accuracy' and 'carelessness which is extremely disturbing'.

Another ground, alleging the appellant purchased food grains from various shops under fictitious names, was found to be vague because it lacked specific details like shop names or dates, making it impossible for the appellant to make an effective representation.
The court found that at least two grounds were vague and one was false.
law: While courts cannot question the sufficiency or reasonableness of the grounds for detention (which is based on the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority), they must scrutinize the material on which the decision is based.
The grounds for detention must be precise and provide sufficient details to allow the detenu to make an effective representation.
If some of the grounds supplied are found to be non-existent, false, or vague, the entire detention order is vitiated and cannot be justified.

The court cannot separate the valid grounds from the invalid ones to determine if the valid grounds alone would have been sufficient. To do so would be to substitute the court's objective judgment for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority.
application: The Court applied the legal principles to the facts of the case, noting that the detention order displayed multiple defects.
It identified the ground concerning the 'pending case' as non-existent or false, given the appellant's prior acquittal. This demonstrated a lack of due care by the detaining authority.
It also identified other grounds as being too vague to allow the appellant to make a meaningful defense.
Because some of the grounds were false and others were vague, the Court concluded that the entire basis for the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction was flawed.
Following its own precedent, the Court held that since the detention order was based on a mix of valid and invalid grounds, the entire order must be struck down.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court accepted the appellant's argument, concluding that the grounds of detention were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, and based on carelessness. The Court ruled that these defects made the detention illegal, allowed the appeal, and ordered the appellant's release.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the court can scrutinize the material on which the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority is based, even if it cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds.
appellant_arguments: The appellant challenged the grounds of detention, arguing that some did not exist in fact and others were vague or irrelevant, implying that the court has the authority to scrutinize them on these parameters.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's defense of the grounds, such as claiming facts existed even after an acquittal, implies that the court should accept the authority's subjective satisfaction and not scrutinize the underlying material too deeply.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a detention order can be sustained if one of the grounds supplied is found to be non-existent, vague, or irrelevant.
appellant_arguments: The appellant's challenge to individual grounds as being non-existent, vague, or irrelevant implies that the entire detention order is vitiated if any of the grounds are found to be defective.
respondent_arguments: The respondent's attempt to defend each ground individually, even those that were weak (like the one based on an acquitted case), suggests a belief that the detention order could be sustained even if one ground failed.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the grounds of detention supplied to the appellant were vitiated by being non-existent, vague, or based on carelessness.
appellant_arguments: The grounds were non-existent, vague, or deficient.
One ground was based on a case in which the appellant had already been acquitted months earlier, making it false or non-existent.

A ground alleging the purchase of paddy for smuggling was vague because it lacked essential details like names of shops and dates of purchase, making it impossible to make an effective representation against it.
The authority jumped to conclusions without proper inquiry, such as relying solely on a truck driver's statement.
respondent_arguments: The grounds were 'fairly particular and generally well-founded'.
The facts related to the ground involving the acquittal were not non-existent ('non est'), as they existed prior to the acquittal.
The detenu had full knowledge of the facts of the acquitted case and was therefore not handicapped in making a representation.

cases.principle: If a detention order is based on multiple grounds, and one of them is found to be irrelevant or illusory, the entire order is vitiated. A court cannot substitute its own objective judicial test for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority by concluding that the remaining valid grounds are sufficient to sustain the order.

cases.case_name: Keshav Talpade v. The King Emperor
cases.principle: If a detention is based on multiple grounds and one ground is found to be invalid, the detention on the grounds which survive cannot be allowed to stand.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: If a detention order is based on multiple grounds, and one of those grounds is found to be irrelevant, non-existent, or illusory, the entire detention order is vitiated as a whole. A court cannot uphold the order by determining that the remaining valid grounds are sufficient, as this would substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority.
obiter: The formation of an opinion for preventive detention rests on the subjective satisfaction of the executive authority, and courts cannot act as an appellate authority to review the sufficiency of the grounds.
The grounds for detention must not be vague or indefinite and must provide a real opportunity for the detenu to make a representation.
Detention without trial is a serious matter that requires the greatest circumspection by the authorities in forming their decision.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The appellant's detention is illegal because the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority was based on multiple grounds, some of which were non-existent, false, or vague. When any of the grounds supplied to justify a detention order are found to be defective, the entire order is vitiated. The court cannot sever the invalid grounds and uphold the detention on the remaining ones, as it is impossible to assess how each individual ground contributed to the authority's subjective satisfaction, and to do so would be to substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive.
legal_tests_applied: If one of several grounds for detention is found to be non-existent, irrelevant, or vague, the entire detention order is vitiated, as the court cannot substitute its own objective test for the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.
Grounds for detention must be sufficiently precise and furnish enough details to allow the detenu to make an effective representation; otherwise, the detention can be questioned.

While the court cannot act as an appellate authority on the sufficiency of the grounds, it can scrutinize them to determine if they are non-existent, false, vague, or the product of carelessness, which would invalidate the detaining authority's subjective satisfaction.
policy_considerations: Powers of detention without a trial must be exercised with the greatest care and attention, and a disregard for truth and accuracy in formulating the grounds is a matter of great regret.

Allowing a court to uphold a detention order by severing bad grounds from good ones would be to substitute an objective judicial test for the subjective decision of the executive authority, which is against the legislative policy underlying preventive detention statutes.
